3.text: They are long, thin tubes¹ (Fig. 155, d², e¹), inside of which the needles,

4.text: thrust into a piece of rag or of thin leather, are kept.

5.text: The thimble is slipped on a thin strip of leather fastened to the needle-

6.text: case, and prevented from falling by a thimble-

25.text: Pouches for holding snuff-boxes and sundry

26.text: small implements are often worn on the belt (see

27.text: Plate XXIII, Fig. 1). Their shape resembles that

28.text: of American Eskimo specimens. For instance,

29.text: that represented in Fig. 156 is similar to specimens

30.text: from Alaska in the National Museum at Wash-

31.text: ington. Other pouches and small bags are made

32.text: of a seal’s flipper or of a swan’s foot. Instances

33.text: like this are met also on the American shore.

34.text: Bone or ivory combs are used for shredding

35.text: grass needed for insoles, and for preparing sinew

36.text: to be used as thread. Usually the combs have two

37.text: prongs Fig. 157, a), and are shaped quite like those

38.text: used in Alaska.⁴ Some, however, have several prongs (Fig. 157, b) or a circular

39.text: head with prongs around it and a wooden handle inserted (Fig. 157, c). These are

40.text: more like other kinds of Eskimo combs used for removing loosened hair from skins.⁵
